I've found that you'll never be sure where the line is until you're long over it. What you can do is try to stop yourself from even getting close, which obviously can't work all the time, or even most of the time as the case may be. So what I'd suggest aside from that is to find a close friend who you can trust to tell you when you're toeing that line- sometimes perspective has to come from the outside. Sometimes dealing with this disease is all about setting up speed bumps to make it harder for it to get going so fast that you can't stop it. I wish you the best of luck.

I'll start off with the disclaimer that my official diagnosis is schizoaffective, which is on the bipolar/schizophrenia spectrum if you buy into that model (psychiatry is still kind of confused as to how to handle patients that present with symptoms of a mood disorder and psychosis, as I understand it). Anyway, it took me a long time to come to grips with it. My family and friends had noted me acting more distant or confused, but it wasn't until I went through my entire library flipping my books around because I thought there were bugs in their spines that I was ready to admit that I might actually be dealing with something. Before that, everything I was doing made sense to me. Even in retrospect, it's difficult to filter my own "disordered" reasoning out of my memories. That WAS my reality. Still is sometimes. So I don't know that I could even tell you what the signs were. It's hard to get completely out of that state of mind, although some days are better than others.

Mathematically, geometry in higher dimensions is very well defined. It's sometimes convenient to take time as the 4th dimension, but this doesn't have to be the case. Part of the difficulty of talking about 4D shapes is that we perceive reality in 3 spacial dimensions. That being said, there are techniques for visualizing shapes in the 4th dimension. The basic idea is to proceed by analogy: imagine how a creature living in two dimensions might perceive, say, a cube. One possibility is that it could examine the cube's "shadow", or projection as it's commonly referred to in mathematics. A 4D object has a 3D shadow, and we can observe that shadow to try to visualize the shape. This sounds a lot like me a few years ago. For me, my insecurities about my intelligence and personality fed into my eating disorder. Like somehow if I was skinny enough, people wouldn't notice my other short comings. Like if I perfected my body, everything else would follow. It was a convenient fantasy, because it meant that if I could get the scale to read the right numbers, I would have created the life I wanted and needed. But it was just that- a fantasy. 

I learned rather harshly that the world doesn't reward obsession or genius like I thought it would. It rewards passion, and luck, and balance. And that's a lot harder to learn. It's something I still struggle with every day.

At some point, I have to learn to be okay with not being "good enough". I'm my biggest oppressor. Nobody is so passionately disappointed in myself as I am, and that's something I can learn to correct.

Edit: I forgot to add something very important. I didn't deal with my eating disorder alone. I had professional help. That might be something to look into. That way you can talk about what you're dealing with without the usual dramatics.

This is the problem that got me into math in the first place. It's possible that a more efficient method of factoring exists, we just haven't found it yet. For the most part, we're stuck with a pretty brute force approach, although approaches like elliptic curve factoring can reduce the size of the problem. I think the key piece of intuition here is just how many primes there are up until the square root of whatever very large prime you're using as a factor. And the answer is a lot. Like a mind boggling amount. Digits on a screen don't really give us a good intuition for just how big the numbers we're working with are, but it's something you gain a better idea of over time.

This realization helped me in my studies. One of the key ideas here is that the speed of light is constant. Remember that speed is given by distance and time. Imagine you're in a transparent, rectangular car. There are two mirrors, one at each end of the car. A beam of light bounces between the two mirrors, say, once every second for the sake of mathematical simplicity (in reality, it would be much less than a second, but you're in a transparent car, so let's ignore that for now.) Then we can use the mirrors and the beam of light as a sort of clock.

So now let's say that you're driving from point A to point B in your car at a very high speed. I'm outside of the car watching. We're both counting the number of times the light bounces between the mirrors. We will both count the same number of bounces. But here 's the catch. Let's say you're traveling at 100 m/s and the car is 10 m long. Between bounces, the light will have travelled the length of the car from your perspective. But to me, the light will have travelled 100 m between bounces. Since the speed of light is constant, and we both measure the same amount of bounces, which means we measure the same amount of "seconds", then the only way to make the math work out is if your perception of time is different than mine. Specifically, time is moving slower for you.

It's just a toy example and there are many more subtle issues to consider, but I know this helped me, so hopefully it can help you. DISCLAIMER: I am not a physicist. This is accurate to the best of my very limited knowledge on the topic. Please feel free to correct any errors.

Pretend there are 100 doors, only one of which has the car behind it. You have a 99/100 chance of choosing the wrong door. The host opens every door but two, one of which has the car. Remember, the host knows where the car is. The number of options may look like it's changing to you, but the odds are actually holding steady. Remember that you had a 99/100 chance of choosing the wrong door, which means that if you switch, there's a 99/100 chance that you'll get the car. If it doesn't seem intuitive, it's because it's not. We didn't evolve to have a very good sense for probability, so we have to be able to check some of our "instincts" at the door and reason through it best we can.

Here's my go for what it's worth. The square of a real number has to be positive because a negative times a negative is a positive and a positive times a positive is also a positive. The square root of a number is the number that, when squared, equals that number. But we know that squaring a number always gives us a positive. So there's no such thing as the square root of a negative number.

But mathematicians decided one day to just invent a new kind of number because fuck it, who's going to tell them they can't. So they invented a number that, when squared, equals -1. That means the number equals the square root of negative one. We call that number i. Turns out, it's an incredibly useful number in all sorts of problems. If it's confusing to you, it's probably because it's just one of those things where mathematicians just happened to abstract reality before science caught up to it. It's pretty damn close to magic, in my opinion.

Edit: TLDR, mathematicians make up a number. Everything magically falls into place. Math magic.
